opus-5.5.text:
Research is mostly uncertainty. When you start a project, you usually don't know whether the question even has a clean answer, whether the approach you've picked is the right one, or whether someone already solved it in a paper from the 1970s that nobody reads anymore. A huge part of the job is navigating that fog, and that's where I've found these models genuinely useful.

The first thing is the literature. In physics, and in black hole physics especially, results are scattered across decades, in different notations and conventions. Before, figuring out whether something was known could take days of digging. Now I can describe the idea in my own language and ask whether it connects to anything existing, and often the model points me to the right thread. It isn't always right, so I check, but it shrinks the search space dramatically.

The second thing is speed of iteration. Uncertainty in research is often "I don't know if this calculation will work out." You might spend a week on an integral or a perturbation expansion only to find it's a dead end. If I can sketch the problem and have the model attempt it, or at least tell me whether the structure looks tractable, I learn much faster which directions are worth my time. Failing faster is a real advantage, because most ideas don't pan out, and the sooner you know that, the sooner you can move on to the ones that do.

And I think there's a more subtle benefit: it's a sparring partner. Science is social. You test ideas by talking them through with colleagues, but colleagues aren't available at two in the morning when you have a half-formed thought. Being able to articulate an idea and get pushback, or have the model say "have you considered this limit?", helps you clarify your own thinking. Sometimes the act of explaining the problem is what unlocks it.

What it doesn't do, at least not yet, is replace the judgment about what's worth working on, which questions are deep and which are just technically hard. That taste is still very much on the human side. But for the day-to-day uncertainty of "is this true, is this known, does this work," it's changed how I do research. It doesn't make the uncertainty go away, but it makes it a lot easier to move through.

r001.rationale: The response describes uncertainty about both whether a question has an answer and whether an approach is right, but does not distinguish a known research goal from uncertainty about the path to reach it.

r002.rationale: It says the researcher can sketch a problem and have the model assess whether its structure looks tractable, helping identify worthwhile directions before spending a week on the calculation.

r003.rationale: It says the model is not always right, but checking its suggestions still shrinks the literature search space dramatically.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that uncertainty is really the defining feature of research. If you knew the answer, it wouldn't be research. So for me the question isn't whether a tool removes the uncertainty, it's whether it helps you move through it faster and with a little more confidence about where you're standing.

In my own work on black holes, a lot of the day-to-day is this: you have a calculation that's maybe two hundred lines of algebra, you've made some assumption three pages back, and you're not sure if the weird result you're staring at is physics or a sign error. Historically you'd go knock on a colleague's door, or you'd just grind through it again yourself. What I've found is that having something like ChatGPT to think out loud with, to say "here's what I did, here's what I got, does this smell right to you," is genuinely useful. Not because it's always right, it isn't, but because it's a tireless interlocutor. It'll check the limiting case you forgot to check. It'll say "did you mean to drop that term." And sometimes it'll suggest a reference or a technique from a neighboring field that I wouldn't have known to look for.

The other piece, which I think is underrated, is the exploratory phase. Before you commit to a direction, you want to survey the landscape: what's known, what's been tried, where are the open questions. That's a phase where you're maximally uncertain and often most reluctant to bother a busy expert. Being able to have a conversation that gets you to a rough map in an afternoon instead of a few weeks is a big deal, especially for students.

Now, I'd add a caution. The way I use it well is as a collaborator whose claims I verify, not as an oracle. It has to earn trust the same way a new postdoc does. And when it's wrong, it's often wrong fluently, so you have to keep your own judgment switched on. But honestly, that's the same discipline good science has always required. The uncertainty doesn't go away. You just get a better companion for it.

r001.rationale: The response describes research as uncertain but does not distinguish knowing the goal from knowing which path will reach it.

r002.rationale: It says ChatGPT can map what is known and open questions before choosing a direction, but does not say it can sketch where a proposed approach might lead.

r003.rationale: The response says ChatGPT is useful as a tireless interlocutor even though it is not always right, and stresses verifying its claims.

astra-6.text:
A lot of research is figuring out what question you should even be asking. You have an idea, you try something, it doesn’t work, and you have to decide: Is the idea wrong, or did I just approach it the wrong way?

I think ChatGPT can be useful as a partner in that process. You can explain your reasoning, ask it to challenge an assumption, or explore a simpler version of the problem. Sometimes just having to articulate where you’re stuck helps you see the next step.

But you have to distinguish between generating a plausible suggestion and establishing that something is true. You still need to check the calculation, test the prediction, and confront the evidence. The exciting possibility is that it helps us explore more ideas while keeping that discipline.

r001.rationale: The response separates choosing the research question from deciding whether an idea is wrong or the approach needs changing.

r002.rationale: It suggests challenging assumptions and exploring a simpler problem, but does not say ChatGPT can sketch where a proposed approach might lead.

r003.rationale: It calls ChatGPT a useful partner for exploring ideas while distinguishing plausible suggestions from established truth, conveying value despite preliminary guidance needing verification.

sol-6.1.text:
A lot of research is figuring out what question you should be asking. You have an idea, you try something, it doesn’t work, and you have to decide: Is the idea wrong, or am I just approaching it the wrong way? I see ChatGPT as a useful partner in that process. You can explain where you’re stuck, ask it to challenge an assumption, or explore a different approach.

The important thing is that it doesn’t remove the uncertainty. You still have to check the calculation and judge whether an argument makes sense. But it can help you turn a vague feeling of being stuck into a concrete next step. And sometimes that’s exactly what you need to keep a research project moving.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing a research question and whether an idea or approach is wrong, but it does not clearly distinguish knowing the research goal from knowing the path to reach it.

r002.rationale: It says ChatGPT can challenge assumptions or explore another approach, but does not say it can sketch where an approach might lead before the researcher works through it.

r003.rationale: The response calls ChatGPT a useful partner and says its guidance should be checked, but does not clearly state that preliminary guidance can be valuable even when it is incorrect.
